newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine's impending sugar shake-up baffles trade.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine's impending sugar shake-up baffles trade.

text.p: A Ukrainian government plan to shake up its sugar sector by reducing beet sowings, doubling domestic prices and selling sugar abroad at world prices makes little sense, Western traders said on Friday.
"What it means I don't know. It's very unclear, as usual," said one trader.

Deputy Prime Minister in charge of agriculture Mykhailo Zubets -- also appointed agriculture minister this week -- told reporters on Thursday that Ukraine would take the steps to reform its inefficient and supply-glutted sugar market.
But traders said the measures, which Zubets said would cut excess supplies domestically and reduce contributions to an already full world market, were unrealistic on several counts.
"They say they want to charge world prices on world markets. Does that make Russia a world market?" the trader said.
Ukraine exports most of its sugar to Russia, and smaller amounts to former Soviet republics.
"If they try to sell at world prices internationally, that will lead to world prices for the domestic market," he said.
Ukrainians earn on average $80 per month.

Ukraine's agriculture is still largely run in the Soviet style with strong government control, and frequent handouts to impoverished producers involve bartering seeds and sugar for supplies like fuel and machinery.
Zubets did not say by how much sugar beet sowing would be reduced this year, but he said domestic demand for refined sugar was 1.5 million tonnes annually.
Ukraine produced 3.26 million tonnes of refined sugar from its last crop and 3.49 million in 1995/96.
"Price supports here don't work," said another Western trader."They (the government) don't need to do anything except to stay out of it. Then it would be an excellent market."

Another Western trader said the idea of charging higher world prices and using the money to reform the sector was about two years old -- a brainchild of state sugar concern Ukrsukor, which was dissolved this year and has not been replaced.

"But the money would not be used for that -- it would be used to support the refineries," the second Western trader said, adding that at least 50 of Ukraine's 191 refineries -- many built at the turn of the century -- were so inefficient that they should be closed.

Privatisation of refineries has been almost non-existent, and British sugar producer Tate and Lyle is to shut a refinery it spent $5 million modernising in the port city of Odessa after the government banned sugar cane imports.
The second Western trader also said Ukraine was forced to sell to former Soviet republics because its refined sugar was below European standard. "It's an isolated market," he said.
A Russian Foreign Trade Ministry group called last August for quotas on refined sugar imports of 1.5 million tonnes in 1997, with Ukrainian supplies capped at 1.15 million.
The trader estimated there was an excess of about 300,000 tonnes of sugar left, which refineries were holding in order to buy fuel when production begins again next year.
He also said sowing would probably be lower this year because Ukraine's steadily declining agriculture sector was suffering from even greater shortages of seed, fuel and machinery than last year.
